Canada Tariffs, Again
 
Plus, a new Iran sanctions campaign and a shrunken Shein
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
GEOFF ROBINS/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Trump threatened new tariffs on Canada. President Trump said the U.S. would impose 50% tariffs on automobiles, auto parts and steel from Canada starting in January, the latest escalation in a tit-for-tat trade conflict that erupted over the weekend. The threat came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would respond to a separate set of Trump’s tariffs. Trump imposed those new tariffs—effective on about 5% of Canadian exports to the U.S.—early on Saturday, after last-minute talks fell apart.

 

Bessent launched a new economic-isolation campaign against Iran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the U.S. was sanctioning more than 60 entities, individuals and vessels across the world that enable Iran to procure nuclear and missile technology, earn revenue from oil and carry out cyber operations. But it was unclear how the sanctions initiative would treat China, a major economic partner of Iran that buys around 90% of the oil it exports.

 

Stocks were mostly lower. The S&P 500 traded down 0.3% and the Nasdaq fell 0.8, led down by chip stocks. Nvidia ended the day down 2.9%, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 2.7%. U.S. automakers, who have extensive trade and production ties to Canada, fell on the newly announced tariffs. Ford, General Motors and Crysler-owner Stellantis dropped 3.3%, 1.1% and 4.8% respectively.

 

Shein priced its initial public offering well below initial hopes. The Hong Kong stock sale could now value the Chinese fast-fashion company at around $27 billion, down from the $100 billion valuation it once boasted. Despite the watered-down price, Shein’s IPO is set to be one of the biggest in Hong Kong this year.

One Big Story

 
 
ANDREW THOMAS/CNP/ZUMA PRESS
 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s mission to tame the bond market could get help from another Trump administration push: crypto legislation.

 

The connection is that under the Genius Act—the crypto regulatory law passed last year—stablecoins issued in the U.S. that aim to stay fixed to the value of the dollar can back that promise only with certain assets, including Treasurys that mature within 93 days.
